entry.title: madvise, Or Talking Back to the Kernel
entry.content:
In the OPT post I ended up at madvise() as the thing that already exists for "telling the kernel about the future", and I kept reading about it after, because it's kinda the only place in Linux where user space is officially allowed to have an opinion about its own pages. Everything else about virtual memory is the kernel deciding and you not knowing.

int madvise(void *addr, size_t length, int advice);

You give it a page-aligned range and a flag, and the kernel does something, or nothing, depends on the flag. That "or nothing" part is what makes it interesting to me.

hints that are actually hints

MADV_SEQUENTIAL and MADV_RANDOM describe how you're going to touch a file-backed mapping, so the kernel reads ahead more aggressively for sequential and basically turns readahead off for random. MADV_WILLNEED says I'll need this range soon, and for a file mapping the kernel starts reading it in asynchronously so the fault later is cheap (or doesn't happen). These are the polite ones, the kernel can ignore them and your program is still correct, just maybe slower.

MADV_HUGEPAGE is in the same family. If THP is set to madvise mode (common on servers), only ranges marked with this get huge pages, so it's an opt-in, and MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is the opt-out for the cases where huge pages hurt you, which happens more than people expect.

and one that is not a hint at all

MADV_DONTNEED sounds like the polite "I don't need this anymore, reclaim it if you want", but on private anonymous memory Linux throws the pages away right now, and the next access gets a fresh zero page.

size_t len = 64 << 20;
char *p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
               MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
memset(p, 'a', len);

madvise(p, len, MADV_DONTNEED);
printf("%d\n", p[0]);   // 0, the 'a's are gone

So it's a free that keeps the mapping, which is actually useful (allocators use it exactly for this), but it's a command with a hint's name. POSIX has posix_madvise(POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) which is supposed to be a real hint, and glibc on Linux just makes it a no-op, I'd guess because mapping it to the Linux one would silently destroy data in programs written for the POSIX meaning. lol.

MADV_FREE and the RSS confusion

MADV_FREE (4.5) is the lazier version. It tells the kernel these pages are garbage, but it doesn't drop them until there's memory pressure, and if you write to the page before that happens the kernel just cancels the free and keeps it. For an allocator this is nicer, because a lot of freed memory gets reused soon and with DONTNEED you'd pay a fault plus zeroing every time.

The problem is RSS doesn't go down. The pages are still counted against you until the kernel actually reclaims them, so tools and people looking at top think the program is leaking. Go switched its runtime to MADV_FREE and then switched back to MADV_DONTNEED by default a few versions later, mostly because of this, people saw memory "not being returned" and the monitoring and OOM decisions around containers believed RSS. I find that kinda funny, but I get it, if every dashboard shows the process growing nobody cares that the memory is technically free.

COLD and PAGEOUT

MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT came in 5.4 and these are closest to the OPT thing. COLD moves the pages to the inactive list so they're first in line for reclaim, while PAGEOUT reclaims them now, anon pages go to swap and clean file pages get dropped. Neither destroys data, the next access just faults it back in.

These came from Android, where the system knows an app went to the background long before the kernel's LRU figures it out. Which is the "the app knows more than the kernel" argument again, except the knowledge comes from the system watching the app, and the app itself doesn't say anything. And for that there's process_madvise() (5.10), which lets one process give advice about another process's memory through a pidfd. Only a few flags are allowed there (COLD, PAGEOUT, WILLNEED, COLLAPSE I think) and you need CAP_SYS_NICE plus ptrace-level access to the target, which makes sense, letting random processes push other people's memory to swap would be a fun attack.

This also kinda answers the trust question I had in the OPT post. Plain madvise only touches your own memory, so the worst a bad hint can do is hurt you, and the kernel doesn't need to trust you at all. The moment advice crosses a process boundary it needs permissions. I'm not sure that's a designed principle or it just happened that way, but it works.

the weird ones

Some flags aren't about caching at all and feel like they ended up in madvise because it was the syscall that takes a range. MADV_DONTFORK keeps a range out of the child after fork() (RDMA buffers need this), MADV_WIPEONFORK gives the child zeros instead of a copy, which is nice for RNG state or keys you don't want two processes to share by accident, and MADV_DONTDUMP keeps a range out of core dumps. MADV_MERGEABLE opts the range into KSM. MADV_POPULATE_READ / WRITE prefault the range so you don't take the faults later, which is basically MAP_POPULATE but for an existing mapping.

At this point it's less "advice" and more a drawer for per-range memory flags. I don't think that's bad, but the name stopped meaning much a while ago.

what I think about it

The thing I like is how small the leak in the abstraction is. The default is still the kernel deciding everything, and most programs never call madvise and that's fine. The programs that do call it are mostly allocators, runtimes, databases and Android, people who already know their memory better than the kernel and want a way to say so without taking over (which is what O_DIRECT and buffer pools do).

What's missing for me is anything with a notion of time, all of this is "now" or "soon" or "not anymore", nothing like "I'll need this in 10 seconds". Would the kernel even do anything useful with that? no idea, maybe not.

notes

  • addr has to be page-aligned, length gets rounded up to pages.
  • MADV_DONTNEED on shared or file-backed mappings doesn't zero anything, the next access just reads from the file/page cache again. The zeroing is the private anonymous case.
  • MADV_FREE only works on private anonymous memory.
  • MADV_COLLAPSE (6.1) synchronously collapses a range into huge pages instead of waiting for khugepaged.
  • MADV_REMOVE frees the backing store for shmem/tmpfs ranges, it punches a hole.
  • man 2 madvise is honestly pretty readable for once.

entry.title: Should malloc Know About Tiered Memory?
entry.content:
This started as a side thought in advanced systems class, we were talking about OS transparency in general and I kept coming back to malloc afterward, because it's the abstraction I use the most and never question, so this is me chewing on it more than a full argument.

malloc is blind

When you call malloc() you get a pointer, and the allocator has no idea if the physical page behind it is fast local DRAM or slower CXL-attached memory. glibc's allocator was built for a world where memory is mostly uniform, so it worries about arenas, chunks, brk vs mmap and lock contention, and leaves physical placement completely to the kernel. That was fine when the latency gap between memory was small, but machines now can have 2-3x differences between tiers, and from user space memory still looks flat.

the kernel fixes it later

The way tiered memory is handled today is the kernel treats slow memory like another NUMA node, watches which pages get accessed, and moves hot pages up to fast memory and cold ones down. It works, but it's always the same shape, allocate first, observe later, migrate if needed, so the system is always reacting.

And migration isn't free, you copy pages, update page tables, flush TLB entries, and if the kernel guesses wrong about what's hot you pay all that for nothing. I keep wondering how much of this goes away if the allocator just knew something before placing the memory.

the app already knows

void *hot_table = malloc(1 << 20);   // frequently accessed
void *log_buffer = malloc(1 << 20);  // rarely accessed
void *archive = malloc(100 << 20);   // mostly cold

Same call, same path as far as glibc is concerned, but these three are completely different in how hot they are. The application usually knows this already, and we throw that away and make the kernel figure it out again from access bits and sampling. Or even worse, trying to build AI models to handle this for us.

So one idea, not exotic at all, is to let the allocator take intent:

void *malloc_hot(size_t size);
void *malloc_cold(size_t size);

malloc_hot() could bind to the fast node using what already exists like mbind() and set_mempolicy(), and malloc_cold() goes straight to the slow tier, so instead of allocate, detect, migrate, you just place it right the first time and skip a lot of the copying.

is transparency still worth it here?

Virtual memory exists to hide where your bytes physically live, that's the whole point, but once the latency gap gets big enough placement starts mattering again whether we like it or not. You can keep it fully hidden and let the kernel grow more sampling and migration machinery, or leak a bit of the abstraction and let developers say hot or cold.

I don't know which is better tbh. Hints sound clean until people start labeling everything as hot because why not, and then what, the kernel ignores the hint? overrides it silently? Once you expose placement you also hand out responsibility for it, and I don't think most developers want that, even the ones who complain about performance.

Huge pages make it messier too. Inside one 2MB page only a small part might be hot, so moving the whole thing to fast memory wastes space, and the allocator doesn't even know how its allocations line up with huge page boundaries, the kernel can split or merge them later anyway. Page size, allocation and tier placement used to be separate concerns and they kinda aren't anymore.

I don't think transparency should go away, most programs don't care about this level of performance. But it doesn't have to be all or nothing, the default can stay hidden like today, and for the stuff that matters the allocator takes hints while the kernel keeps the right to override them when they're bad, or punish them!!!

entry.title: Why Databases Stopped Using mmap
entry.content:
After writing about buffer pools the obvious question was why not skip all of it, mmap the data files, touch pages through pointers, and let the kernel's page cache decide what stays in memory. That deletes thousands of lines of buffer pool code, and a lot of databases tried it, LMDB, LevelDB, MonetDB, MongoDB's old engine, and SQLite has an mmap mode. Most of them backed away later.

the kernel writes when it wants

This is the one that kills it for anything transactional. The kernel can flush a dirty mapped page whenever it wants, so a change you made through the mapping can hit disk before the transaction commits, or before its WAL record is written, and a crash at that moment leaves the database inconsistent. A buffer pool doesn't have this problem because the page sits in the database's own memory until it decides to write it, log first, data second.

People found workarounds and they're all a bit sad. MongoDB's MMAPv1 used MAP_PRIVATE as a copy-on-write scratch space, which means two copies of the data in memory. SQLite copies pages into user buffers before modifying them, which is most of a buffer pool again. LMDB uses shadow paging, which works but means one writer at a time. Every fix gives back the simplicity mmap was supposed to buy.

stalls you can't schedule

When a mapped page isn't in memory, touching it faults and the thread blocks until the disk read finishes, and there's no async version of a page fault. A buffer pool can issue reads with io_uring, and a B+tree range scan can prefetch the next few leaf pages before it needs them. With mmap the same scan faults on every cold page, one at a time. madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL) helps a bit for scans, but it's a hint and its readahead behavior is a kernel detail that changes between versions.

errors become signals

With a buffer pool there's one place where pages come in, so you check the checksum and handle I/O errors there. With mmap a page can be evicted and reloaded behind your back at any time, so in theory you'd verify checksums on every access, and an I/O error during that reload doesn't return anything, you get SIGBUS. Now your error handling is a signal handler, which is a horrible place to do recovery from.

and it doesn't even scale

I assumed at least the performance would be good, the kernel's paging code is old and well tuned. A group at CMU (Crotty, Leis, Pavlo) benchmarked it in 2022 and it's pretty bad. In their random read test the dataset was much bigger than memory, and mmap started fine, then throughput dropped to almost nothing once the page cache filled and eviction started, and it recovered to about half of what plain O_DIRECT reads got. For sequential scans over 10 NVMe drives mmap stayed around 3 GB/s while direct I/O got ~60 GB/s, and mmap barely improved going from 1 drive to 10.

The reason is eviction. Each evicted page has to be removed from the TLB of every core that might have it cached, which means sending interrupts to other cores (TLB shootdowns), and under heavy eviction that happens millions of times a second. Reclaim also runs mostly in one kswapd thread per NUMA node, and every faulting thread fights over the same page table. So the bottleneck is inside the kernel's eviction path and adding faster drives doesn't move it.

who backed out

MongoDB deprecated MMAPv1 in 2015 and removed it in 2019, InfluxDB moved off mmap after big I/O spikes once databases got past a few GB, and RocksDB started as a LevelDB fork partly because of LevelDB's mmap bottlenecks. Others (Scylla, TileDB, VictoriaMetrics) looked at it early and decided not to.

It's still fine when the whole dataset fits in memory and you mostly read, since eviction never really runs and the write ordering problem doesn't come up much, and that's roughly where LMDB lives. Past that, I think the general lesson is the same one from the buffer pool post, the kernel's page cache doesn't know about transactions or access patterns, and the database does.

notes

  • The paper is "Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?" (CIDR 2022), it's short and readable.
  • TLB shootdowns are also what makes page migration expensive in other places, same mechanism.
  • PostgreSQL never used mmap for data files, it has shared_buffers.

entry.title: A Buffer Pool Is Just Paging in User Space
entry.content:
The first time I looked at how a database buffer pool works I had this weird feeling I'd seen it before, and I had, it's the same thing the kernel does with pages, frames, page tables, eviction and dirty pages, just written again in user space. And the databases do it on purpose.

same pieces, different names

A buffer pool is an array of page-sized frames, plus a hash map from (file, page number) to frame, which is the database's page table. When a query wants a page it checks the map, and if the page is there it pins it and gets a pointer back. If not, it picks a victim frame, writes it out first if it's dirty, reads the new page in, updates the map. That's a page fault handler, it just runs in the database process and never traps into anything.

Each frame has a dirty flag and a pin count, and a pinned frame can't be evicted, same idea as the kernel's reference count on a page.

OS virtual memorybuffer pool
page frameframe
page tablehash map page id -> frame
page fault handlermiss handler
dirty bit in PTEdirty flag
reference countpin count
kswapd / reclaimeviction (LRU, clock)
swap / filedata file

so why not let the OS do it

You could just mmap the data file and let the kernel handle all of this, and some databases tried, it didn't go well. The kernel's page cache is general purpose, so it doesn't know which pages are index pages, which are part of a scan that will never be touched again, and which can't hit disk yet.

That last one matters most I think. With write-ahead logging the log record has to be on disk before the data page it describes, so before the buffer pool writes a dirty page it checks that the WAL is flushed up to that page's LSN. The kernel has no idea what an LSN is and flushes dirty pages whenever it wants, and if it flushes a page before its log record and you crash at the wrong moment, recovery is broken. You can't fix that with a hint, you need to own the write-back.

Eviction is the other thing. A sequential scan touches every page once, and plain LRU would let that scan push out the hot index pages. PostgreSQL gives big scans a small ring of frames so they cycle through a few slots instead of polluting the whole pool, and InnoDB puts new pages in an "old" part of its LRU and only promotes them if they get touched again. And the database can prefetch the next leaf pages of a range scan because it knows it's doing a range scan, while the kernel only sees file offsets.

O_DIRECT

If the database has its own cache and also reads through the kernel, every page lives twice in memory, once in the pool and once in the page cache. So InnoDB and others open files with O_DIRECT and skip the page cache completely. It's annoying to use, buffers and sizes have to be aligned to the block size or you get EINVAL, so everyone ends up writing their own aligned allocator.

PostgreSQL is the odd one, it still goes through the page cache and relies on fsync, so it double caches and shares control with the kernel. I'm not sure if that's a deliberate tradeoff or just history, probably both, and I think there's been work on direct I/O there but I don't know how far it got.

notes

  • PostgreSQL's pool is shared_buffers, with clock-sweep eviction.
  • SQLite has its own page cache on top of the OS one and doesn't care, small databases don't suffer much from double caching.
  • Concept is simple, details are brutal (latches, concurrency, I/O scheduling), and it's one of the first things people build in database courses.

entry.title: Swap and Paging: What Actually Happens When Memory Fills Up
entry.content:
Swap is basically a disk pretending to be RAM, when memory fills up the kernel pushes some pages out to disk and brings them back when someone touches them again. That's the whole idea and it sounds boring, but it's the reason a machine can go from fine to frozen mouse in a few seconds, so I wanted to write down what actually happens in between.

faults, the cheap kind and the expensive kind

When you touch a page that isn't mapped, the CPU traps and the kernel goes to find it. If the page is already somewhere in memory (page cache, a shared mapping, a page that was never touched and just needs a zero page) the kernel fixes the page table and you're back in microseconds, that's a minor fault and it happens all the time, lazy allocation and copy-on-write are built on it. If the page has to come from disk it's a major fault, and your thread just sits there.

AccessLatency
RAM~100 nanoseconds
SSD~100 microseconds
HDD~10 milliseconds

SSD is around 1000x slower than RAM and HDD around 100,000x, so one major fault doesn't matter, a hundred per second and the app feels sluggish, a thousand and the system is basically gone.

picking a victim

When RAM is full and the kernel needs a frame, it picks some page that wasn't used recently. If it's clean (a file page nobody modified) it just drops it since it can read it again from the file, and if it's dirty it has to write it somewhere first, file pages go back to their file and anonymous memory (heap, stack) goes to swap, because it has nowhere else to live. That's kinda why swap exists at all, without it anonymous memory can never be evicted and the kernel can only throw away file cache.

The ideal would be evicting the page needed furthest in the future (OPT), but nobody knows the future, so Linux keeps active and inactive lists and reclaims from inactive first. Tracking exact access times for every page would cost too much, so it's closer to "touched recently or not" than real LRU.

thrashing

If what you're actively using is bigger than RAM, every page you load pushes out another page you need soon, which then faults back in and pushes out the first one, forever. The system spends almost all its time moving pages and almost none doing work, and that's the stuck mouse. More swap doesn't fix it btw, it just lets you get deeper into it before the OOM killer shows up.

knobs

/proc/sys/vm/swappiness (default 60, range 0-200) is how willing the kernel is to swap anonymous memory vs dropping file cache. Low keeps your app memory and sacrifices cache, high swaps more and keeps cache warm. I don't think there's a right value, people argue about this forever.

Then overcommit, which lets malloc(1GB) succeed with 512MB free because most programs ask for more than they touch. The allocation succeeding means nothing, the OOM killer fires later when you actually use it. Mode 0 (default) is a heuristic that still refuses obviously crazy requests, 1 always says yes, and 2 is strict accounting that breaks a lot of software.

And some memory can never be swapped at all, kernel memory (who would page the kernel back in?) and anything pinned with mlock, which RDMA and databases use.

the part I actually care about

Disk is the slow part, and the paging model itself is fine. So one idea is to keep paging exactly as it is but swap to another machine's unused RAM over the network instead of disk. With RDMA that's a few microseconds, slower than local RAM but way faster than SSD, and the cliff when you run out of memory becomes more of a slope.

Linux used to have a hook for this called frontswap, where a module could catch pages on their way to swap and put them somewhere else, and remote memory systems plugged in there. I think it got removed a couple of years ago (6.5?) and zswap now hooks in directly, so I'm not sure what the clean way to do this is today. Need to look into it, different post.

notes

  • Pages are usually 4KB, huge pages (2MB, 1GB) exist to cut TLB misses.
  • vmstat, sar, /proc/meminfo to watch paging. si/so in vmstat is swap in/out.
  • zswap compresses pages in RAM before they hit swap, buys some time.
  • Swap on SSD is fine, swap on HDD is pain.

entry.title: mmap: Mapping Files into Memory
entry.content:
mmap is one of those calls where the API is tiny and what happens behind it is most of the virtual memory system. You ask for a file (or just zeroed memory) to show up in your address space, you get a pointer back, and from then on you read and write the file like an array without any read() calls.

int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDONLY);
struct stat st;
fstat(fd, &st);

char *p = mmap(NULL, st.st_size, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
// p[0..st.st_size-1] is the file now

nothing is loaded

The part that took me a bit to accept is that mmap doesn't read anything. The kernel just creates a VMA (a note saying "this range of addresses belongs to that file at that offset") and returns, so the actual loading happens later when you touch a page, it faults, the kernel pulls that page into the page cache, points your page table at it, and you continue like nothing happened. Second touch is a normal memory access, no kernel involved at all in it, and that's why it can be faster than read(), there's no copy into a user buffer and no syscall per access.

private vs shared

This is the flag that actually changes meaning. MAP_PRIVATE is copy-on-write, you read the file's pages but the first write gives you your own copy and the file never sees it. MAP_SHARED writes go into the page cache pages themselves, so other processes mapping the same file see them and they reach disk eventually, and "eventually" means whenever the kernel feels like it unless you call msync.

Add MAP_ANONYMOUS and there's no file at all, just zero pages. glibc malloc does this for big allocations (over 128KB by default), which is nice because munmap gives the memory straight back to the kernel, while memory from brk can only shrink from the top of the heap. Anonymous plus shared gives you memory that survives fork as shared between parent and child, and shm_open + mmap does the same for unrelated processes.

where it's good and where it hurts

It's good for reading big files with random access, and for read-only stuff many processes use, since they all map the same page cache pages, ten processes mapping a 1GB file don't cost 10GB. Shared libraries are loaded this way, and JITs use anonymous mappings with PROT_EXEC.

It hurts when you need control. The kernel decides when dirty pages hit disk, a page fault blocks your thread and you can't make it async, and if the file shrinks under you or the disk throws an I/O error you get SIGBUS instead of an error code, which is kinda horrible to handle. For databases all of this adds up, enough that most of them stopped using it. And for small files I don't think it's worth it, setting up the VMA and taking faults probably costs more than one read(), though I never measured it.

Appending to a file is also awkward, the mapping has a fixed size so you ftruncate to grow the file and remap, and at that point write() is just simpler.

notes

  • MAP_POPULATE prefaults everything at map time, so mmap gets slow but later accesses don't fault.
  • MAP_FIXED puts the mapping at your exact address and silently replaces whatever was there. MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE is the safer one.
  • PROT_NONE pages are good as guard pages, mprotect changes protection later.
  • MAP_HUGETLB for huge pages, less TLB pressure.
  • madvise() tells the kernel how you'll access the range (MADV_SEQUENTIAL, MADV_RANDOM, MADV_WILLNEED).
  • Exiting without munmap is fine, the kernel cleans up. Long-running stuff should unmap tho, or VMAs pile up.

entry.title: OPT, and telling the OS about the future
entry.content:
In one of the lectures the instructor was going through cache replacement policies, LRU, FIFO, clock, the usual ones, and then he mentioned OPT, which is the one that is actually optimal and also the one nobody can implement. I wrote "blame OS transparency?" next to it in my notes and it stayed there for sometime, so this is me finally looking at it.

what OPT does

When the cache is full and you need a slot, OPT evicts the page whose next use is furthest in the future, and a page that is never used again is the perfect victim. Belady showed in 1966 that this gives the minimum number of misses (that's why it's also called MIN, or Belady's algorithm, same thing). The problem is the kernel would need the future access sequence and it obviously doesn't have it, so OPT ends up as a measuring stick where you record a trace, run OPT on it offline, and see how far LRU or clock is from it.

my lazy thought

The kernel only sees page faults and accessed bits, it has no idea my program is about to scan a 10GB file once and never touch it again, or that some table will be hit again in two seconds. But the program kinda knows that. So why can't it just tell the kernel something like "this page, I'll need it much later", or even hand over the path the code is going to take and let the kernel do something closer to OPT?

I thought I was onto something, and then found out people did this a long time ago.

it already exists, sort of

Linux has madvise() for memory and posix_fadvise() for files, and they're basically this idea in a very coarse form. MADV_DONTNEED / POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED say I'm done with this, MADV_WILLNEED says I'll need it soon so go prefetch, MADV_SEQUENTIAL and MADV_RANDOM describe the pattern, and newer kernels (5.4 I think) added MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT which mean "this is cold, deactivate it" and "just reclaim it now". POSIX_FADV_NOREUSE was a no-op on linux for years, I think it got wired up to something recently but I haven't checked how much it actually does. And mlock() goes the other direction and pins pages so they never get evicted.

None of these say "next use is at time t", they're more like near vs far, but ranking near vs far is most of what OPT needs anyway, if the hints are honest that is.

Databases skipped the conversation completely, they open files with O_DIRECT and run their own buffer pool because they have the query plan, and a query plan is a pretty good description of the future.

On the research side this was a 90s thing. Cao, Felten and Li had application-controlled file caching where the kernel decides how much cache each process gets and the process decides which of its own blocks to drop, and Patterson et al. had informed prefetching and caching where the app discloses its future accesses to the kernel, which is literally the "give the OS the path" line from my note lol. Exokernel went all the way and said the OS shouldn't hide resources at all, just multiplex them safely and let apps manage, so breaking transparency was not exactly a new idea, MIT built a whole OS around it.

why it's still not OPT

The page cache is shared, so even if my program tells the kernel its exact future, global OPT needs everyone's future and the other processes aren't saying anything. The 90s work handles this by splitting it, the kernel does allocation between processes and each app does replacement inside its own share, which is reasonable, but you only get something close to OPT inside your own slice.

There's also trust, because if hints affect eviction then every app will say its pages are important. I'd guess that's part of why mlock is capped by RLIMIT_MEMLOCK. Hints that evict your own stuff sooner are safe to honor, hints that push other people's stuff out are not.

And the program often doesn't know the future either, which ngl kills most of my original idea. A scan or a loop over an array is predictable, but anything that branches on data, or waits on user input or the network, has a path that depends on values you don't have yet. You could hand the kernel probabilities instead, but then you're predicting again, which is what LRU already does.

One more thing that bugged me, OPT minimizes misses and not cost. Evicting a dirty page means a write while evicting a clean one is free, and when objects have different sizes (CDNs) the whole problem changes, so even perfect knowledge of the future doesn't give you the best policy in the sense you actually care about.

where OPT actually runs

It runs wherever the future is known. Register allocation is one, when the compiler has to spill inside a basic block it can pick the value whose next use is furthest because it sees all the code, and that's Belady again with registers instead of pages. DNN training is another, the compute graph is fixed so you know exactly when each tensor is needed, and systems that swap tensors between GPU and host memory plan around that.

Then there's learning from OPT, which I like more than the hint stuff. Hawkeye (CPU caches) runs OPT over past accesses and trains a predictor to guess whether OPT would have kept a new line, and LRB does something similar for CDNs. You can't know the future, but you can look at the past, ask what OPT would have done, and hope the future looks similar enough.

So would breaking transparency solve it? partially, for programs that really know their access pattern, and those mostly already took the cache away from the kernel. For general stuff I don't think it helps much, because the app usually doesn't know its future either. Not sure what a hint for "data-dependent future" would even look like.

notes

  • Belady, "A study of replacement algorithms for a virtual-storage computer", IBM Systems Journal, 1966.
  • Cao, Felten, Li, application-controlled file caching, USENIX 1994.
  • Patterson et al., "Informed Prefetching and Caching", SOSP 1995.
